segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted” slowly and put it in my own words: Lady Catherine asks whether Pemberley's shades are to be polluted by Elizabeth's family. Next, craft. I notice her grand, insulting language, as if Elizabeth were a disease. The strongest word is “polluted”: it treats Elizabeth's family as dirt. Then, effect. What does Lady Catherine fear? My answer: Lady Catherine fears that Elizabeth's low connections will disgrace Pemberley if Darcy marries her; her snobbery is exposed, and her visit will instead show Darcy that Elizabeth has not refused him.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the chapter for characterization, dialogue (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this chapter suggest about the great confrontation? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Chapter LVI develops the idea of the great confrontation. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of conflict and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: Elizabeth's refusal to obey Lady Catherine asserts her right to choose her own happiness. When the text says “I am only resolved to act in that manner which will, in my own opinion, constitute my happiness” (Chapter LVI, paragraph 68), it shows this directly. She is "only resolved to act in that manner which will, in my own opinion, constitute my happiness," rejecting rank as a reason for obedience.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.
